title: AI Agent Skills for App Marketing: How to Build Reusable Workflows
summary: AI agent skills turn repeatable marketing work into reusable playbooks. Learn how skills differ from prompts and MCP, plus a SKILL.md template for app teams.
body_markdown:
Every team has their share of repeatable tasks, workflows, and processes. There’s the daily checks, the weekly reviews, a launch checklist. An AI agent skills can help gather information that has been scattered across various platforms and documents, saving time and effort.


This was the main topic in a recent ROI 101 episode featuring Eldar Agayev, founder of Hatchly. He discussed using AI skills alongside connected marketing tools in order to achieve a practical and automated process for repeatable work. In the podcast, Eldar explains different uses for AI agent skills, how to feed it better definitions and instructions for viable output, and how to create safe boundaries for review and action.


## **What are AI Agent Skills?**


AI agent skills are reusable guidelines for a particular task, usually saved as a folder with a skill.md file. This file contains instructions for how an AI agent should perform. It starts with a short metadata block (at a minimum, a name and description) followed by plain language instructions. For many app marketing teams, a skill can define data sources, steps, metric definitions, output format, when to review output, and certain limitations. A skill can also include scripts, reference documents, or templates.


Eldar explains:


> “Skills are prompts that are saved as files that AI knows a short description of and can run when needed.”


According to the[Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io/home) documentation, agents load skills in three stages:


1. **Discovery:** the agent reads only the name and description of each available skill.
2. **Activation:** when a task matches a description, the agent loads the full instructions.
3. **Execution:** the agent follows the instructions and uses any bundled files or connected tools it needs.


Having a detailed and comprehensive description is vital for skill creation. It is the only reference the agent reads when deciding whether or not to use a skill.


Originally developed by Anthropic, the Agent Skills format was released as an open standard. Many AI tools support it, but discovery and setup still vary by client, so test a skill in the AI tool your team uses.


For an app marketing team, a skill might cover:


- A morning acquisition and revenue review
- A campaign audit before a budget decision
- A subscription-health summary
- A creative-learning review across channels
- An app-store review triage process
- A market-research checklist for a new country or category


Rather than replace a marketing strategy, skills are more intended to enhance your work by making the operating standards easier to apply for your team across the board. Skills are not supposed to replace a marketing strategy. However, a good skill can enhance the strategy by making the operating standards easier to apply consistently.


## **Prompts, Skills, and MCP Servers**


A prompt is an instruction for one conversation.


A skill is a saved instruction set for a recurring task.


An MCP server gives the agent access to tools and data. Most useful marketing workflows combine a skill with one or more MCP servers.


**Prompt** **AI agent skill** **MCP server**


**What it is** A one-time instruction typed into a conversation A reusable instruction set saved as a file A connector that exposes tools and data to an AI app


**Answers the question** What do I want right now? How should this task be done every time? What can the AI access?


**How it is reused** Copied and pasted by a person Found by the agent when a task matches its description Available whenever it is connected


**Best for** Exploration and one-off questions Repeatable work where output quality matters Bringing live data and actions into the workflow


**App marketing example** “Summarize yesterday’s campaigns” A daily growth review with set sources, cohorts, and flags Access to attribution, ad-network, or subscription data


A skill isn’t necessary for every single question. A one-off analysis can be used within a prompt. A skill is most useful when the task repeats and the quality of the output matters enough to define the process.


“Summarize yesterday’s campaign performance,” would be a good example of a prompt. A skill based on a daily review would go much further: it tells the agent which sources to check, which cohorts to compare, how to flag unusual changes, which metrics to include and when to stop to ask a human for context.


## **Generic Skills, Generic Results**


It can be very easy to simply copy and paste a popular prompt. It’s also tempting to just copy and paste a skill template. However, whatever is easy and accessible is probably something every other competitor can easily do too.


Instead, a skill should truly reflect the way your team works. It should be bespoke and unique to your brand and types of problems you want to solve.


> “If everyone will copy the same design skills or the same marketing skills, then the whole marketing design is going to be the same.”


Templates are useful for starting out and testing. They provide a foundational structure, but the real advantages start once you provide bespoke detail and inputs. This information could be about:


- Your app’s audience and value proposition
- The metrics that signal quality, not just volume
- The countries, platforms, and channels you prioritize
- Your definition of a healthy cohort or a worthwhile test
- Your brand voice and creative constraints
- The actions an agent can recommend, prepare, or take


A generic “write five ad ideas” skill gives generic output. A specific creative review skill can ask the agent to identify the audience, message, proof point, platform, test hypothesis, and success metric before it produces anything.


## Build These Three AI Agents First


Your first skill should not be the most ambitious project. It should be one that is repeatable and can remove friction from a process.


### 1. The Daily UA Review


This skill pulls together approved data sources and answers:


- What changed since the previous report?
- Which campaigns or sources need attention?
- Did spend, installs, activation, revenue, or subscription signals move together or apart?
- Are there obvious data-quality or app-health issues to investigate?
- Which decisions need a human review today?


Try to keep the output short with a summary and actionable steps. Ask for the evidence behind the analysis and include a list of open questions. This should be able to provide more clarity for how to go about your day.


### 2. Campaign Planning with Improved Questions


An agent cannot produce a useful acquisition plan if the request is “to test a new angle” and nothing else. It operates based on the knowledge and specific context that a team would have.


Eldar shared a skill he calls “Grill Me,” designed to ask for that missing context before the work begins. It can ask about geography, the creative hypothesis, success criteria, data sources, and what has already been tried.


This is a valuable pattern for app marketing. Build a planning skill that asks:


- Which audience are we trying to reach?
- What problem or product benefit should the creative communicate?
- Which country, platform, and channel are in scope?
- What would count as success?
- What is the kill criterion?
- What evidence from earlier tests should shape this one?


When asking for this kind of information, it helps your team transition from vague request to testable hypothesis.


### 3. Creative Learning


If the review process is clear, then creative outputs are able to move faster and faster. A creative learning skill can sample from the existing approved results and organize the next test around the audience, message, format, and product moment. It can use those learnings to produce an approved asset faster.


Ask the skill to separate facts from suggestions:


- Observed: What performed for a comparable audience or campaign?
- Interpretation: What pattern may explain the result?
- Hypothesis: What should be the next creative test?
- Guardrail: What claim, brand element, or targeting approach must be avoided?


This makes the agent’s reasoning easier to review and helps the team avoid turning a single result into a broad rule.


## How to Structure an AI Skill


Don’t overthink this yet. A long, technical document is not the only pathway to creating a useful skill. A simple and clear Markdown file is all you need to start. To help you structure your input, try organizing your data into seven parts:


**Section** **What to include** **Example for a campaign-review skill**


**Name and purpose** The job the skill performs “Daily mobile acquisition review”


**Trigger** When it should be used (this goes in the description) “Use when the team asks for a morning performance summary”


**Inputs** Approved data sources and required context Spend, attribution, revenue, subscription metrics, app version


**Steps** The order of work Compare age-matched cohorts, identify changes, check anomalies


**Output** The format the team wants Three findings, evidence table, recommended next review


**Rules** What the agent must and must not do Do not change budgets. Label forecast value separately from observed revenue


**Escalation** When to ask for help Ask if the attribution window, target, or test criterion is missing


By using this structure, your instructions are easily inspectable and understood. It becomes easier for your team for review, improve upon it, and understand why an agent took a certain path or how they reached a particular recommendation.


### An Example of a SKILL.md Template for a Daily Review


It’s important to always adapt the sources, metrics, and thresholds to your own team. The values in brackets are placeholders.

---


name: daily-acquisition-review


description: Builds a short morning review of mobile app acquisition performance. Use when someone asks for a daily performance summary, a morning report, or "what changed since yesterday" for paid user acquisition.


---


# Daily acquisition review


## Inputs


-   Attribution and cost data from [  MMP  ] for the previous day and the prior 7 days


-   Subscription events (trials, new subscribers, renewals, cancellations) from [subscription platform]


-   Current app version and release date


## Steps


1.   State the reporting period, apps, countries, and platforms included.


2.   Compare yesterday against the prior 7-day average for spend, installs, activation rate, and day-0 revenue.


3.   Compare cohorts only at the same age (for example, day-3 vs. day-3).


4.   Flag any metric that moved more than [  X%  ] and list the campaigns that drove the change.


5.   Check whether a new app version shipped in the period.


## Output


-   Three findings, each with the supporting numbers and source


-   A table of campaigns that need review, with the reason


-   Open questions for the team


## Rules


-   Read-only. Do not change budgets, bids, or campaign status.


-   Label observed data, interpretation, and recommendations separately.


-   Label predicted LTV as a forecast, never as observed revenue.


## Escalation


-   If a data source is missing or a date range is incomplete, say so and stop. Do not estimate missing values.

## Connect Skills to Tools


A skill only goes so far as to describe how an agent should perform. In order for an AI agent to work properly, the agent still needs approved access to the data and tools required for the job.


Let’s consider a subscription health skills minimum context requirement. It may need campaign and attribution data, subscription events, and some other metrics. On the other hand, a release review skill needs another type of content: app store status, recent reviews, and error signals. The connection layer (usually an MCP server) gives the agent access to those inputs.


Learn more about MCP servers for app marketing and how to connect the data and tools to your skill. We recommend starting off with read only data for your first few skills and slowly adding controlled write actions only when your process is stable, the permissions are appropriate, and the team has a clear approval process.


## How to Test and Improve Skills


Your first version won’t be perfect and that is completely fine. Try it out a few times on days that you already know the answer and then ask:


- Did it use the right sources?
- Did it surface the information the team actually needs?
- Did it confuse observed data with a forecast or recommendation?
- Did it ask for context at the right time?
- Were the output and tone useful for the person reading it?
- Did it stay inside its allowed scope?
- Did the agent load the skill when it should have? If not, rewrite the description.


Then update the instructions. Small changes, such as a better metric definition, a more specific escalation rule, or a clearer output format, can make the next run more useful. Keep skills in a shared folder or repository so the team can see what changed and why.


This iterative approach is more reliable than trying to write one “perfect” master prompt. It also gives your team a durable record of how it makes recurring decisions.


## Common Mistakes for AI Skills


- **A vague description.** “Marketing helper” doesn’t give the agent much to go on. Be specific about what the skill does and when to use it.
- **Trying to do everything in one skill.** Keep each skill focused. A daily review and a creative brief need different steps and outputs.
- **Leaving metrics undefined.** Define terms like cohort age, attribution window, and revenue type so the agent doesn’t have to guess.
- **No guidance on when to stop.** Explain what the agent should do when data is missing, such as asking for clarification or flagging the gap.
- **Overloading the instructions.** The Agent Skills specification recommends keeping the main SKILL.md under 500 lines. Move detailed reference material into separate files so the core instructions stay easy to follow.


## Key Takeaways About Agentic Skills


- A prompt asks the agent to do something once. A skill saves a workflow the agent can reuse whenever a matching task comes up.
- Agent Skills are an open format originally developed by Anthropic and now supported by many AI tools.
- Generic templates are a starting point Adding your own metrics, audience, and decision rules makes the output more useful.
- When building a skill, cover seven things: its name, when to use it, the required inputs, steps to follow, expected output, rules, and when to ask for help.
- Skills tell the agent how to do the work, MCP servers connect it to the data and the tools it needs.


## Build Skills to Preserve Human Judgement


AI agent skills work best when they make your existing expertise easier to apply. They should not flatten your marketing into generic recommendations or hide the decisions that need human judgment.


Start with one workflow. Define the audience, sources, rules, and output. Review the first runs together. Then \[run the workflow as part of a daily marketing operating process or flow, then (/blog/ai-marketing-agents-mobile-apps/) when you are ready to turn recurring analysis into controlled, reviewable work.


## Frequently Asked Questions About AI Skills


**What is a SKILL.md file?**


A \`SKILL.md\` file is the core of an agent skill. It starts with YAML metadata, including a name and a description, followed by Markdown instructions that tell the agent how to perform the task.


**Are AI agent skills the same as prompts?**


They are related but not the same. A prompt is typed for a single conversation. A skill is saved, reusable, and loaded by the agent when a task matches its description. Skills can also bundle scripts and reference files.


**Do skills work across different AI tools?**


Agent Skills is an open format, and many AI tools support it. Discovery, installation, and tool access still differ by client, so test each skill in the tool your team uses.


**Do I need to code to create a skill?**


No. A basic skill is a Markdown file written in plain language. Coding helps only if you want the skill to include scripts.


**What is the difference between a skill and an MCP server?**


A skill tells the agent how to do a task. An MCP server gives the agent access to the tools and data the task requires. A daily reporting workflow typically uses both.


**How many skills should a marketing team start with?**


Start with one. Pick a task your team repeats weekly or daily, build the skill, review a few runs together, and add the next one once the first is reliable.
